8.0.0.en: Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said: [1]

8.0.1.en: How long wilt thou speak these things?

8.1.0.en: And shall the words in thee (thy words) be a strong wind! [2]

8.1.1.en: In sharp heat Bildad tries to silence Job's mouth and criticizes his emotional outburst. Bildad flared up and attacked Job: "How long wilt thou speak these things?" as though he were saying that the words of Eliphaz were entirely sufficient, and that Job ought to have kept silent and submitted. He likened Job's revolt to a violent, stormy wind, but it will not be able to stand before divine justice.

8.1.2.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that Bildad rushed headlong in his attack on righteous Job; for had he kept silent and been patient he would have realized that what Job said was nothing but a natural reaction to the severe sufferings and trials into which no one else had fallen. Moreover, even in his reproach of God, he did not deny that he was a sinner who asks His forgiveness. But Bildad's babbling, or his rashness in speech, made him fall into condemning the righteous man and into exaggerated criticism, so that he saw evil in the righteous man's good words. Bildad did not realize that a suffering man's expression of the weariness he sees is something that human nature necessarily requires.

8.1.3.en: * Did he (Job) say that he suffers injustice?

8.1.4.en: Behold, you (Job's friends) have not reached your goal in any way, for he never said this. But Job spoke of the weakness of his nature, saying, "Am I a sea, or a whale?" (Job 7:12), "Is my strength the strength of stones?" (Job 6:12) What is my life? [For I shall not live forever, that I may bear with patience] (Job 7:16). Besides this, he knew his sins: "Why dost thou not pardon my transgression?" (Job 7:21)...

8.1.5.en: After that, Bildad condemned himself in his babbling, for he failed to understand that those who actually experience pain find comfort in expressing themselves, since Job himself said: [I also will not restrain my mouth, for I am in distress] (Job 7:11). In any case, he says that these words with which I speak are required by necessity.

8.1.6.en: * The golden vessel is not used for base things because of its high price; how much more the mouth, which is more precious than gold and coral, so that we must not defile it with foul speech, cursing and the slander of others.

8.1.7.en: St. John Chrysostom * The words of the righteous are always grievous to the unjust, and what they hear for edification they carry as a burden on their shoulders. This is what Bildad the Shuhite plainly indicates about himself when he says: "How long wilt thou speak these things?" He who says "How long" shows that he is not yet able to bear words of edification.

8.1.8.en: The unjust boast greatly that they say what is right, and they find faults in good sayings...

8.1.9.en: When criticism is exaggerated, the discourse certainly loses its meaning...

8.1.10.en: The wicked blame good things, lest they themselves be seen not to know what is good.

8.1.12.en: Holy Scripture, like the Fathers, has warned us of the sin of Bildad: rash babbling in speech, which gave rise to condemnation and to exaggerated, biting criticism:

8.1.13.en: "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise" (Prov 19:10).

8.1.14.en: "For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool's voice is known by multitude of words" (Eccl 3:5).

8.1.15.en: "For in the multitude of dreams and many words there are also divers vanities: but fear thou God" (Eccl 7:5).

8.1.16.en: * The Apostle did not say that there is no one who tames the tongue, but that no one (of men) can tame the tongue; even once it has been bridled, we confess that this is by the tenderness of God's grace and His help.

8.1.17.en: * A man can tame wild beasts, but his tongue he cannot bridle...!

8.1.18.en: A man can train everything except himself; he has no power over himself!

8.1.19.en: He is able to train everything that he fears, or ought to fear, but as for himself, whom he does not fear, he has no power over him!

8.1.20.en: Therefore let us take refuge in God, who is able to bridle it. You cannot persuade your tongues because you are men... Let us ask God to tame us, saying to Him: "Lord, Thou hast been our refuge."

8.1.21.en: Can (man), the image of God, tame the lion, while God is unable to tame His image?

8.1.22.en: Our hope lies in this Tamer, that we may submit to Him, seeking His mercy... Let us bear with Him until He tames us, and we become perfect, for He often allows us chastisements. If you use whips in taming wild animals, does not God use them to turn us, His wild beasts, into His children?

8.1.23.en: St. Augustine * Babbling is the throne of vanity, and from this throne appear the love of self-display, boasting and bragging.

8.1.24.en: Babbling is a sign of ignorance, the door of slander, a guide to jesting and laughter, and a servant of lies and hypocrisy.

8.1.25.en: * It is a proof of drowsiness and a scattering of memory; it removes watchfulness, cools fervor and weakens prayer.

8.1.26.en: St. John Climacus * Beware of the babbling tongue and of the two eager ears (for hearing news). Do not belittle others, and do not listen to one who belittles another.

8.1.27.en: St. Jerome * Do not be hasty with your tongue, for the mouth is a snare of death.

8.1.28.en: The so-called Barnabas * He who guards his tongue shall never be robbed of his treasure. The mouth of the silent man interprets the mysteries of God. And he who speaks hastily becomes distant from his Creator.

8.1.29.en: The Spiritual Elder * We must not use rebuke except rarely. And if we are compelled to use it, we must strive eagerly to serve God and not ourselves.

8.1.30.en: Let us have one aim, and let us do nothing with a double heart. Let us take out of our eyes the beam of envy or malice or pretence, so that we may be able to see and take the speck out of our brother's eyes. Let us look at the speck with the eyes of the dove, which belong to the bride of Christ (Song 1:4), whom God chose for Himself as a glorious Church without spot or wrinkle, that is, pure, without guile (Eph 27:5).

8.1.31.en: St. Augustine * Do not be a judge of your brother, that you may be made worthy of forgiveness; you may perhaps see him always in error, but you do not know with what end he will depart from the world. For the thief crucified with Jesus was a murderer and a shedder of blood, and Judas was a disciple of Christ and one of the intimates, since the money box was with him, yet in a short time they changed, so that the thief entered Paradise, while the disciple deserved the gallows and perished.

8.2.s.en: 2. God is just in what befalls believers

8.2.0.en: 3 Doth God pervert judgment? or doth the Almighty pervert justice? 4 When thy children sinned against him, he delivered them into the hand of their transgression.

8.2.1.en: Doth God pervert judgment? or doth the Almighty pervert justice? [3]

8.2.2.en: Bildad reckoned that Job's revolt was an outburst against God, as though God perverts judgment and reverses the right. Far be it from anyone to think this. Man in his weakness may resort to reversing the right because of his fear, but God is "the Almighty"; He is neither unjust nor does He do what is false.

8.2.3.en: * The blessed Job did not deny this in his speech, nor was he ignorant of it when he held his tongue. But all the insolent speak well-known truths in grand words in order to show by this that they are learned.

8.2.4.en: They disdain to keep their peace in a spirit of humility, lest they be thought silent through ignorance. Yet it is well known that they praise the uprightness of God's justice when they themselves are safe from calamities and enjoy the prosperity of their lives while others suffer disasters.

8.2.5.en: They walk in evil, and yet they think themselves righteous. Being in prosperity, they imagine that this is by virtue of their merits, and conclude that God does no injustice... But if a power of correction (by discipline) touches their lives even to the slightest degree, they at once rush to attack the divine government, though a little before - since no harm had touched them - they were lavish in praise and admiration of the divine providence.

8.2.6.en: They refuse to admit that any judgment is just when it falls upon them... Well does the Psalmist speak against the confession of the wicked: [He will praise thee when thou doest good to him] (Ps 49:18)... For this reason we do not wonder that Bildad praises the justice of God so long as it does not touch him personally.

8.2.8.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in Job's friends a symbol of the heretics, for when they see the holy Church in tribulation for her edification, they reckon that what has befallen her is a matter of divine justice, and that the prosperity they enjoy is on account of their virtues.

8.2.9.en: Often the enemy of good supports the heretics in every age with material means and temporal honor, in order to ensnare the children of God from the bosom of the holy Bride, at one time by dazzling, deceptive philosophies, at another by material enticements, and a third time by keeping them from the tribulation that the Bride, the partner of the Crucified, endures.

8.2.10.en: This is the role of Bildad, who in his ignorance imagined wisdom, and reckoned Job a blasphemer against God the Almighty and a murmurer against divine justice.

8.2.11.en: * (The enemy of good) invented heresies and schisms in order to ruin the faith, corrupt the truth, and destroy unity.

8.2.12.en: And since he is unable to keep us in the dark ways of the new error, he draws us into a new maze of deception.

8.2.13.en: He catches people away from the Church herself, and while they think they have drawn near to the light and escaped the night of the world, he plunges them into a new darkness, of which they are unaware.

8.2.14.en: And although they do not hold to the Gospel and the order of Christ and His law, they claim to be in the light through the deceptive flatteries of the enemy, of whom the Apostle says that he transforms himself into an angel of light and adorns his servants as servants of righteousness.

8.2.15.en: They call night day, death salvation, despair hope, treachery faithfulness, and the antichrist Christ, and he thwarts the truth by deception, by presenting the truth in a false form.

8.2.16.en: This is what happens, my brethren, when we do not return to the fountain of truth, when we do not look to the Head and keep the teaching that comes from heaven.

8.2.17.en: St. Cyprian * It is the habit of the devil to imitate the things that belong to God. He raises up false apostles to oppose the true Apostles, and takes the form of an angel in order to deceive men.

8.2.18.en: Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus * There are philosophers who have skillful discussions about virtues and vices, distinguishing between them and giving definitions of them, and in the end offering a precise logical sequence, filling books, and protecting their wisdom with talkative speeches; these dare to say to people, follow us, join our party if you wish to live happily. But they do not enter by the door; these want to destroy, slaughter and kill.

8.2.19.en: * If we find these three persons, holy brethren, we find those whom it befits us to love, those whom we must bear with, and those of whom we must beware. The shepherd is loved, the hireling is borne with, and the thief is guarded against.

8.2.20.en: St. Augustine * "A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject; knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself" (Titus 10:3-11). May we, like wise sailors, sail in our faith on the sound course so that we may cross most safely, and follow the coasts of the Holy Scriptures.

8.3.0.en: St. Ambrose When thy children sinned against him, he delivered them into the hand of their transgression [4].

8.3.1.en: Bildad tries to provoke Job by ascribing what befell Job's children to the fruit of their sin and evil, so that they received just recompense from God. What inflamed Job's wounds all the more was that Bildad reckoned the death of Job's children in this horrible manner to have no other explanation than that they disobeyed God, so He delivered them into the hand of their transgression. Job had confessed that he was a sinner, and he used to offer burnt offerings in the names of his children lest a sinful thought against God had crossed their thoughts. But it cannot be judged that what happened was the natural fruit of a disobedience they had committed.

8.4.0.en: 5 If thou wouldest seek unto God betimes, and make thy supplication to the Almighty; 6 If thou wert pure and upright; surely now he would awake for thee, and make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous. 7 Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase.

8.4.1.en: Yet if thou wouldest seek unto God betimes, and make thy supplication to the Almighty [5].

8.4.2.en: Bildad offers Job good advice, to hurry and rise early, asking and making supplication to God, but Bildad did not feel that Job deserved to obtain more than what he had. He advises him to pray and petition God so that He may restore to him manifold what he lost, if he is pure and upright.

8.4.3.en: How strange! Bildad offers Job destructive advice that reveals the ruin of Bildad's own heart. He asked him to pray early to the Almighty. This seems excellent scriptural advice, for the believer asks of the Almighty, asks and receives because he rises early to God, but he does not make prayer for the enjoyment of the Giver of gifts but for the acquiring of temporal gifts, reckoning that the answering of prayer by the enjoyment of temporal things is a sign of God's pleasure and of the holiness of the one who prays. It is a dangerous indicator that corrupts faith in God, who wants us to seek the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things are added to us.

8.4.4.en: Nothing prevents us from asking God as our Father for everything, even trivial matters, as a sign of our living fellowship with Him, but the answer, in the obtaining of what we ask, will not be a sign of our sanctification and of God's love for us.

8.4.5.en: Perhaps Bildad here was certain that Job would not recover what he had lost, which would be a sign of his wickedness, like his perishing sons. On the other hand, Bildad sets the measure of righteousness and uprightness as a person's enjoyment of temporal things. Pope Gregory (the Great) says: [Wicked people count temporary pleasures a special blessing of divine reward. What they themselves run after with great care and intense desire, they promise to others as a great thing.]

8.4.6.en: Prayer - in the mind of St. Augustine - is the language of the soul's longing for God. It is the interpreter of the heart's desire.

8.4.7.en: * Prayer is the reaching of the mind, filled with love, to God; it occupies mind and heart, thought and desire, knowledge and love. The whole life of the good Christian is a holy desire.

8.4.8.en: * Alas! It is easy to ask things of God and not to ask God Himself, as though the gift were better than the Giver.

8.4.9.en: * God does not forbid love of these things, but that we find our happiness in loving them. It befits us to make the love of our Creator the goal of our esteem for these things... The dowry is given to the betrothed so that through her dowry she may love him. So God gives you everything; therefore love the One who made them.

8.4.10.en: * What precious thing does he ask of God who holds his esteem of God Himself in contempt?!

8.4.11.en: * Ask nothing of God, but the gift of Himself to you.

8.4.12.en: * To hope for God from God - this is to love God, the Giver of grace.

8.4.13.en: * It is not right to love what comes from God if God Himself is forgotten because of it(a).

8.4.14.en: * You will find nothing that He offers you better than Himself, but if you find what is better than Him, ask for it by every means.

8.4.15.en: * Does God have no reward? There is none but the gift of Himself!

8.4.16.en: St. Augustine Father Aphrahat looks upon prayer as an inner meeting of the pure heart with the Holy God; prayer is the speech of the heart, which will not be an object of delight to the Holy God unless it is pure and clean.

8.4.17.en: * Prayer is beautiful and its works are upright; acceptable prayer makes a person feel rest. Prayer is heard when we feel forgiveness in it.

8.4.18.en: Beloved prayer is pure prayer, free of all guile. And prayer is strong when the power of God works in it.

8.4.19.en: My dear one, I wrote to you that when a person commits himself to fulfil the will of God, and it is the basic axis of his prayer, the person rises high in his prayer. I have told you this: do not neglect prayer.

8.4.20.en: You must long for prayer and not grow weary of it. As our Lord said and it is written: "that men ought always to pray, and not to faint" (Lk 18:1), you must yearn for vigil, and put away from you heedlessness and sleep. You must be awake at all times, by day and by night, and not grow slack.

8.4.21.en: St. Aphrahat * Did Job need this teaching of yours?

8.4.22.en: Was he not praying always throughout his whole life? And you say: [Rise early in prayer to the Lord Almighty].

8.4.23.en: Not only did he not cease to pray early to the Lord, but he offered it early (Job 1:5), and throughout the day and at every moment, he praised God seven times a day (Ps 119:97, 164), by day and by night; for this was not folly to him. The end of his trials shows this, the result of his struggles (which showed that he was a man of prayer)...

8.4.24.en: You have misjudged (O Bildad) and wronged the wrestler, for Job did not fail to see God, of whom you speak in order to criticize the righteous man, and not to glorify God.

8.5.0.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem If thou wert pure and upright; surely now he would awake for thee, and make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous [6].

8.5.1.en: Bildad thinks that if Job were pure and upright, this calamity would not have befallen him, and that if he had acted well at the first trial, the second trial would not have come upon him.

8.5.2.en: This is not right, for a good man may be tried more than once, and may even be exposed to a trial that extends through his whole life, which is counted as nothing when compared with the eternity he will enjoy.

8.5.3.en: Bildad pretended to advise Job to repent of his evil so that God might restore to him what he had been, and even more than he had been, but in his depths he wanted to assure him that he is wicked and a hypocrite.

8.6.0.en: Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase [7].

8.6.1.en: Bildad sees that Job is a wicked man; if he were upright and fell into a trial, his latter end would be better than he was before the trial. Indeed God wanted to prove to Bildad that Job is righteous and upright, so He made his latter end better than his beginning.

8.6.2.en: Job's latter end became more glorious than his children, but what he gained at the end of his life was nothing but a pledge of the glory prepared for him in the eternal life. He died an old man, full of days, but he rises to live eternally in the heavenly Jerusalem.

8.6.3.en: Many martyrs and saints suffered at the end of their lives, but these sufferings and torments are spiritual pearls and jewels whose greatness and splendor we shall recognize on the great Day of the Lord, when they take pride in the love they expressed by accepting sufferings with thanksgiving and joy!

8.7.s.en: 4. The accusation of Job with hypocrisy

8.7.0.en: 8 "Enquire of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers: 9 For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow. 10 Shall not they teach thee, and tell thee, and utter words out of their heart, saying: 11 Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water? 12 Whilst it is yet in his greenness, and not cut down, it withereth before any other herb. 13 So are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish: 14 Whose hope shall be cut off, and whose trust shall be a spider's web. 15 He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand: he shall hold it fast, but it shall not endure. 16 He is green before the sun, and his branch shooteth forth in his garden. 17 His roots are wrapped about the heap, and seeth the place of stones. 18 If he destroy him from his place, then it shall deny him, saying, I have not seen thee. 19 Behold, this is the joy of his way, and out of the earth shall others grow."

8.7.1.en: Enquire of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers [8].

8.7.2.en: Bildad did not dare to declare to Job that what had befallen him - according to his personal experience - is nothing but a confirmation that he is wicked; rather he laid the foundation of this judgment on the experience of the ancient generations. If Eliphaz had relied on his personal experience, Bildad completes that by referring to the experience of the ancients.

8.7.3.en: In his comment on these phrases [8-10], Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem sees that what happened with Job resembles what happened with Abel. Cain looked at the corpse of his brother Abel, lying slain on the ground (Gen 4), and thought that this was the fruit of his deed, and that Cain was righteous, the earth having settled and rested so as to be in his hands while he was in tranquillity, and he did not discover the truth that the voice of his brother's blood cries out, having reached heaven.

8.7.4.en: As Cain looked at Abel, reckoning that what befell him was because of his evil, so Bildad and his companions looked at Job on the dunghill, and reckoned him wicked. And as God bore witness to the righteousness of the slain, declaring that the gates of heaven were open to receive his voice, so God bears witness to Job and listens to the cries of his heart. Cain wanted to trample his brother under his feet, and the friends wanted to crush Job's soul under their feet.

8.7.5.en: It befitted Job's friends themselves to ask the early ages and see that the injustice that befell Abel was not from an evil in him but because of his righteousness, and that his life did not end with earthly blessings and temporal goods, but with the opening of the gates of heaven to receive the cries of his blood shed on the earth.

8.7.6.en: Eliphaz said that God does not allow any of the upright to be destroyed thus (Job 4:7), whereas Bildad says here that God drives hypocritical wicked people to shame, disgrace and ruin in this world. If Eliphaz wanted to assert that Job is not upright, otherwise all this would not have befallen him, behold, Bildad directs to him an outright accusation that he is a wicked hypocrite.

8.7.7.en: He asks Job to resort to the early ages to make sure for himself that what he says is true, through the long practical experience of God's judgments concerning the wicked from the early ages until their own time.

8.8.0.en: For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow [9].

8.8.1.en: He asks him not to rely on his own experience, even if he is an old man, because the whole age is like a day, as though it had passed yesterday, and his knowledge is limited, and his experience is almost as fleeting as his life. This is what drives us to look to the experience of the ancient generations.

8.8.2.en: His words came close to what King David sang in his farewell prayer, saying: "For we are strangers before thee, and sojourners, as were all our fathers: our days on the earth are as a shadow, and there is no hope" (1 Chr 29:15), but his heart and mind were not like David's heart and mind. The words that Bildad uttered are useful, and could have been holy if his heart had been pure, clean, loving and holy.

8.9.0.en: Shall not they teach thee, and tell thee, and utter words out of their heart, saying [10].

8.9.1.en: The early Fathers bear love toward their children and grandchildren, so along with their experience they offer us their wide hearts; therefore their words carry weight.

8.9.2.en: * Bildad set down words of wonderful truth against hypocrites, but in this speech he was pointing to himself. For had he not been pretending to righteousness in a feeble manner, he would not have dared to teach a good man with such great rashness... His words in truth carry wonderful power, but they should have been directed to the foolish and not to a wise man; to the wicked and not to a good man, for he who pours water into the river while his gardens are dry and thirsty shows that he is no less than a madman.

8.9.4.en: I have previously spoken of the importance of the Fathers' heritage in the book "The Beginnings of Christian Patristic Literature", where it says:

8.9.5.en: [To what extent are we committed to what is found in the heritage of the Fathers?

8.9.6.en: The holy Fathers represent the mind of the universal Church, which she received from the Apostles by the action of the Holy Spirit, who works without ceasing in the life of the Church. St. Augustine speaks of them, saying: "They held fast to what they found in the Church, they practiced what they learned, and what they received from the Fathers they entrusted to the hands of the children", "He who despises the holy Fathers knows that he despises the whole Church".

8.9.7.en: This authority rests on two factors: a natural factor, since the Fathers were marked by a holy life and faithfulness in receiving the deposit of the living faith from the hands of the Apostles, and therefore they are better able to bear witness to the life of the Church in all its aspects, especially as they hold one mind, in spite of the differences of cultures, gifts and circumstances, with the great distance between the apostolic sees and the difficulty of communications at that time. And the second factor is divine, in that the Fathers lived enveloped by the Holy Spirit, the Church's leader and guide into all truth, who keeps her within the circle of the Cross of Christ.

8.9.8.en: This does not mean the infallibility of the Fathers as individuals; rather the universal Church as a whole lives preserved by the Spirit of the Lord...

8.9.9.en: The heritage of the Fathers occupied a distinguished place in the life and faith of the Church; St. Athanasius relied on it in his defense, as St. Basil relied on many ecclesiastical traditions through the sayings of the Fathers before him.

8.9.10.en: This tendency, that is, resorting to the sayings of the earlier Fathers, increased in the fourth century and grew greatly in the fifth. St. Cyril of Alexandria, for example, in his writings to the Egyptian monks in defense of the title of St. Mary Theotokos (qeotokoc) - to affirm that the One born is the Word of God incarnate, without separation of the divinity from the humanity - indicated to them that they should follow in the footsteps of the saints, since they kept the faith delivered to them from the Apostles, and taught Christians rightly. Once again he affirms that the correct teaching concerning the Holy Trinity was made clear "by the wisdom of the holy Fathers". And in his discourse against Nestorius he resorted to the teaching of the holy Church extending throughout the whole world and to the honored Fathers themselves, declaring that the Holy Spirit spoke in him. And to support his discourse about the Lord Christ he relied on some patristic excerpts from their polemical writings, which he presented to the Council of Ephesus.]

8.10.0.en: Can the rush grow up without the mire (the marsh)? or can the flag grow without water? [11]

8.10.1.en: As Bildad accuses Job of hypocrisy, he presents painful images of the hypocrite in general, though he means Job in particular:

8.10.2.en: First: the papyrus, which grows only in waters full of mud, and the dry flag that has no water [11].

8.11.0.en: Second: the spider, which relies on its house and thinks it is safe, though its house will not stand [14-15].

8.12.0.en: Third: the grass that the sun burns and dries, though the sun is the secret of the life and growth of plants [16].

8.12.1.en: Fourth: one who stumbles on the stones in the road, and falls and perishes.

8.12.2.en: Fifth: the leafy, beautiful tree whose roots the axe strikes, so that it is uprooted and dies.

8.12.3.en: What is the experience of the early Fathers in this matter? The Fathers answer that the hopes and joys of hypocrites are like papyrus and flag. Both grow in the marsh amid mud or mire or slime, and with water. So the hypocrite does not achieve hope without a stagnant ground or an atmosphere other than mire. He relies on outward appearances of religiosity, piety and success, his appearances being deceptive, on his conceit of himself, on the words of praise directed to him; all these are nothing but mire, and their hopes are nothing but papyrus and flag.

8.12.4.en: If the papyrus points to the hypocritical man, who needs the holy waters of the Holy Spirit: in the midst of the waters the believer is born a son of God by the Holy Spirit, and by the waters of the Spirit he is refreshed and renewed, until he bears the icon of the Lord Christ, and so is made worthy to receive fellowship in eternal glory.

8.12.5.en: * By the papyrus and the flag he points to the life of the hypocrite, for he has the appearance of greenness, but without fruit useful for the service of man; though he is green, he has merely the color of holiness, always dry, practically fruitless...

8.12.6.en: Hypocrites are separated from the Giver of many blessings by the tendencies of the thought of their hearts; while receiving His gifts they seek their own praise, not the glory of the Giver. And while they glorify themselves by praising themselves for the blessings given them, they oppose the Maker of good things by the very gifts.

8.12.7.en: The hypocrite criticizes severely the life of the one who rebukes him. Longing to prove him wrong beyond all limits, so as to justify himself, not by what he practices of deeds but by highlighting the faults of others... Well was it said of Solomon: "Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee" (Prov 9:8)...

8.12.8.en: Here we need to know that the loftiness of the righteous begins in the heart and grows to the end of the present life. But the practices of hypocrites, since they have no roots, often come to nothing before the end of the present life. They often devote their lives to holy studies, and since they do this not to lay up stores of virtues but to obtain praise and flattery, when they reach a phrase that gives them human praise, they are glad of temporal success. Therefore they are altogether empty of holy learning, and they show by their conduct afterward how they love temporal things, while as for eternal things, they go no further than speaking of them with their lips... They are witnesses against themselves that their goodness does not spring from the heart.

8.12.10.en: * For this end the Savior, who had no need of baptism, was baptized, to sanctify the water for those who would be born again.

8.12.11.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * Baptism is called "the washing of regeneration", since it is accompanied by the renewal of the Spirit who hovers over the waters.

8.12.12.en: * The Holy Spirit creates for Himself a new people, and renews the face of the earth, when people through Him put off [their old man with his deeds] (Col 9:3), [and walk in newness of life] (Rom 4:6).

8.12.13.en: * Everyone who is counted worthy of fellowship in the Holy Spirit, through knowing His unspeakable mysteries, will surely obtain rest and joy of heart. For when he has arrived, under the Spirit's guidance, at knowledge of all that happens - how and why it happens - his soul cannot be troubled or feel sorrow.

8.12.14.en: * Human nature is weak. And in order to become strong it needs the help of one who strengthens it. Whose help? The help of the Spirit.

8.12.15.en: That is, he who seeks true strength must become strong by the Spirit.

8.12.16.en: The majority become strong by the flesh and according to the flesh. But the soldiers of God (2 Tim 3:2) become strong by the Spirit, and therefore courageous in facing the fleshly mind [which is concerned with what belongs to the flesh] (Rom 7:8). The spirit is in a wrestling with the flesh, but the spirit of man, which that Spirit strengthens, will win the victory.

8.12.17.en: Origen * The Lord was baptized not to be cleansed but to cleanse the waters, so that when the waters were washed by His body, which did not know sin, they might be used in baptism.

8.12.18.en: St. Ambrose * Christ was baptized, I mean He purified the water by His baptism.

8.12.19.en: Tertullian Whilst it is yet in his greenness, and not cut down, it withereth before any other herb [12].

8.12.20.en: Quickly the papyrus appears with its beautiful green leaves, but it dries up and vanishes in a short time, even before it is plucked up (Ps 129:6).

8.12.21.en: So are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish [13].

8.12.22.en: The secret of hypocrisy is man's forgetting God, who searches hearts and knows the hidden secrets in thought.

8.12.23.en: * [So are the paths of all that forget God, and the hypocrite's hope shall perish]... The hope of the hypocrite cannot stand, for since he does not make eternity his goal, he loses all that he holds in his hand. The inclination of his mind is not fixed on the glory that has no end, but if he pants after passing praise, he loses what he labored to obtain. The "Truth" bears witness to this, saying: "Verily I say unto you, They have their reward" (Mt 6:2).

8.12.24.en: No one can bind himself to the perishing and remain himself imperishable. For he who embraces perishing things naturally descends to perishing. Let him say: "and the hypocrite's hope shall perish".

8.12.26.en: * Job, who was subjected once more to trial, praised God and blessed Him; truly he did not forget God. Therefore the end of the righteous is not compared with the grass that withers in the heat [12]. Since he is like a tree planted by streams of water, that yields its fruit in its season (Ps 1:3), keeping the fruit of virtues, he causes many plantings in the world to flourish.

8.12.27.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * It is a source of joy and glory for men to have children who resemble them... How much more is the pleasure of God when a spiritual man proves in his works and his praises and declares the divine loftiness in his life.

8.12.28.en: St. Cyprian * O soul, He who created you can satisfy you. And if you seek anything else, it is to your misfortune.

8.12.29.en: St. Augustine Whose hope shall be cut off, and whose trust shall be a spider's web! [14]

8.12.30.en: Since the hypocrite does not rely on God, everything he hopes for, and even what he obtains, becomes like the house of the spider, which weaves its delights and consolation in a flimsy web.

8.12.31.en: This text appears in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) as "His folly does not satisfy him..."

8.12.32.en: * It is infinite folly for a man to labor with toil and run panting after a moment of praise, so that a person practices the heavenly commandments with great effort and seeks an earthly wage...

8.12.33.en: "And whose trust shall be a spider's web"... It may happen that the words of hypocrites last to the end of the present life itself, but since they do not seek the praise of their Creator, their works are not counted good in the eyes of God.

8.12.35.en: * [For the hope of the ungodly shall perish, his house shall be without an inhabitant, and his tent shall prove to be a spider's web] (LXX). Why do you say this to Job? Is it because you really know the end of the wrestler, and you have your own view concerning the dweller of his house and his tent as a spider's web?

8.12.36.en: But you think that his house is made of wood and stone, built for him by virtues (Mt 7:24). You imagine his tent made from this earth, and for this reason you think it will perish like a spider's web, whereas his dwelling is really in the heavens, as in the words of Paul: "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven" (2 Cor 5:1-2).

8.12.37.en: For this reason Job also groans, but you (O Bildad) look upon these lamentations as cowardice and blasphemy. He [supports his house] (his trust), not by visible things, but by what is invisible.

8.12.38.en: Therefore Scripture speaks with words of wisdom: [Wisdom hath builded her house for herself, she hath set up her seven pillars] (Prov 9:1)...

8.12.39.en: Job took this with patience, and did not renounce his confidence in his relationship with God; on the contrary, he bore the enemy courageously and repelled his vain attacks, so that he might have a bold face against all conflicts in new attacks.

8.12.40.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Hypocrisy is hated by God and abhorred by man. It brings no reward and is altogether without benefit for the salvation of the soul, but rather is the cause of its perdition.

8.12.41.en: If hypocrisy is sometimes not exposed, it is only for a time, for it does not last long, but everything is revealed, and it brings calamity on its owner, and so it is like a woman ugly in appearance from whom her outward adornment, applied to her by artificial means, is stripped.

8.12.42.en: * Hypocrisy is foreign to the characteristics of the saints, for it is impossible for anything of what we do or say to escape the eyes of the Godhead, for "there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known". All our words and deeds will be revealed on the Day of Judgment. Therefore hypocrisy is wearisome and without benefit. It befits us to be approved as true worshippers who serve God with frank and clear features.

8.12.43.en: St. Cyril the Great * Everyone sees the thief "hypocrisy" carrying everything before his eyes and rejoicing in it! What a new kind of robbery, that draws people and delights them while they are being robbed!

8.12.44.en: St. John Chrysostom He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand:

8.12.45.en: he shall hold it fast, but it shall not endure [15].

8.12.46.en: The hypocrite boasts of his works and relies on them, as the spider holds fast to its flimsy house.

8.12.47.en: As the spider thinks it is fortified by its web, by which it catches its prey, and does not realize that its web can easily be swept away, so the hypocritical man fortifies himself in his formalities and outward appearances of piety and his resources, and behold, he loses everything.

8.12.48.en: * [He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand: he shall hold it up (with a prop), but it shall not endure] [15]. As the house of our outward life is the building in which the body lives, so the house of our thought is whatever the mind concentrates on... for everything we love is for us as though it were a dwelling that gives it rest. Therefore, since Paul set his heart on heavenly things, though he is still on the earth, he is a stranger to it. [Our conversation is in heaven] (Phil 3:20). But the mind of the hypocrite, in all that he does, thinks of nothing but his reputation and fame...

8.12.49.en: The empty soul, finding that it keeps nothing within itself in spite of all its labors, seeks testimony from outside...

8.12.50.en: The hypocrite leans on this house of flattery in vain, for on the Day of Judgment no human testimony will stand. The praise he received as testimony for him he receives as his wage.

8.12.52.en: The Christian, while he walks on earth in a spirit of responsibility and commitment in all that he is entrusted with, bears a heavenly touch in his thoughts as in his feelings and emotions, translated into his words and outward conduct. Our life is a divine school in which we learn and train for the heavenly life, in all the directions of our life.

8.12.53.en: * I want you to keep your minds on these things always (Col 1:3). For our concern with them frees us from the earth and transports us to heaven.

8.12.54.en: St. John Chrysostom * It is right for us to be there in the presence of God in the heavens, we who learned the lesson while on earth, and went there to heaven in order to be in the love of God the Father, whom we came to know while on earth, and because God the Word, the Holy One, made everything and taught us and teaches us everything, and trains us in all good things.

8.12.55.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * When the will of God is accomplished by us who are on earth as it is accomplished by those in heaven, we become like the heavenly ones, as we bear like them the image of the heavenly (1 Cor 49:15) and inherit the Kingdom of Heaven (Mt 34:25). And those after us who are on earth come, praying that they may be like us when we are in heaven (Paradise).

8.12.56.en: Origen He is green before the sun, and his branch (his boughs) shooteth forth in his garden [16].

8.12.57.en: The incarnate Word of God came, the "Sun of righteousness", who rises on those sitting in darkness that they may enjoy the light of righteousness, and become children of light and children of the day. The sun that transfers us from the darkness of the tomb to the light of heaven dries up the grass. This is the work of the Lord Christ, who raised mankind from the death of sin and entered with it into the embrace of the Father, while the deniers who insist on not believing in Him dry up and become fit for the eternal fire.

8.12.58.en: * [He sees it green before the sun comes.] The Lord is often represented in Holy Scripture by the title "the Sun", as was said by the prophet: "But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise" (Mal 4:2). The wicked who are driven away at the judgment are described in the Book of Wisdom: [We have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness has not shone on us, and the sun has not risen on us] (Wis 5:6). Therefore before the sun the papyrus is seen to be green.

8.13.0.en: His roots are wrapped about the heap, and seeth the place of stones [17].

8.13.1.en: The cornerstone raises from us living stones built up in the house of the Lord, in the heavenly Temple. But the wicked stumble over the cornerstone, and fall and perish.

8.13.2.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem uses the Septuagint (LXX), while Pope Gregory (the Great) refers to the Vulgate.

8.13.3.en: * [He falls upon a heap of stones, and lives among flint]... People are referred to in Holy Scripture by stones, as was said to the holy Church by Isaiah: "And I will make thy battlements of rubies, and thy gates of hewn stones (of carbuncle)" (Isa 54:12)...

8.13.4.en: Peter expressed this by offering the counsel: "Be ye also built up as living stones, a spiritual house" (1 Pet 2:5). Here, since he calls them stones, he by no means called them "living stones", but by the bare title of stones; he sets up the lost and the elect mingled together.

8.13.6.en: * [He sleeps on a heap of stones, and dwells among pebbles] These belong to those of whom Isaiah spoke: "Prepare ye the way of the people... clear it of stones" (Isa 62:10). And also: "Prepare the way, take up the stumblingblock out of the way of my people" (Isa 57:14; 1 Macc 5:4; Ps 140:6). He (the enemy) drains himself and wounds himself with an incurable death, when we clear our ways of snares and stumbling stones.

8.13.7.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem If he destroy him from his place, then it shall deny him, saying:

8.14.1.en: He gives another likeness of the hypocrite, the beautiful, flourishing tree, which keeps its greenness in spite of the rays of the sun, and whose roots are firm in the rocky soil, unshaken by the winds. When the axe strikes this tree it is utterly uprooted, and no sign of it remains in the place where it was planted.
